tagline: River canyon views and railroad bridges meet along West Virginia 72
intro: West Virginia 72 follows the Cheat River Byway for 14.3 miles, with little development outside Rowlesburg. The two-lane state highway received its byway designation in June 1996. Pull-offs give views of the river canyon, Buckhorn Run Waterfall and Tray Run Viaduct. The Federal Highway Administration highlights the corridor’s rail and industrial sites associated with mineral extraction, as well as its whitewater recreation.

Railroads made this river crossing strategically important before it became a scenic drive. Rowlesburg took its name from railroad engineer Thomas Rowles. Its Baltimore and Ohio bridges over the Cheat and Tray Run became targets during the Civil War. On April 26, 1863, Union troops and townsmen summoned from church defended the town during the Jones-Imboden Raid.

Dunkard Bottom, on the Cheat River, was the site of the Eckerlin brothers’ Brethren community. At Rowlesburg, the river journey meets a former railroad town with a downtown historic district. The Federal Highway Administration allows 20 minutes to drive the byway, with additional time for recreation and wildlife viewing. The Cheat itself flows north from Parsons past Rowlesburg and Albright, then enters the gorge northeast of Albright.
notice: Roadside pull-offs frame the canyon, Buckhorn Run Waterfall and Tray Run Viaduct.

moments.title: Dunkard Bottom
moments.text: The Eckerlin brothers’ settlement on the Cheat River combined religious life with a trade in animal products. Samuel, Gabriel and Israel had left the Ephrata community in Pennsylvania after a dispute with its founder, Conrad Beissel. When their friend Ezechiel Sangmeister visited in June 1756, he described bearskins used as bedding and counted twenty-eight horses. The community also made maple sugar and sent syrup and sugar to other settlements. It lasted only a few years, ending with the settlement’s destruction in 1757. Sangmeister described the brothers selling furs, meat and tallow to other settlers.

moments.title: Rowlesburg
moments.text: Two railroad bridges made Rowlesburg a military objective: the Baltimore and Ohio crossings of the Cheat River and Tray Run. Confederate troops under General Robert S. Garnett failed to reach the town in 1861. The Jones-Imboden Raid reached it two years later. On Sunday morning, April 26, 1863, Union troops and townsmen called from their churches defended Rowlesburg, and General William E. Jones retreated. The town’s name honors railroad engineer Thomas Rowles. Its downtown historic district was listed on the National Register in 2005. Rowlesburg stands along the Cheat River in southern Preston County.

moments.title: Downtown Rowlesburg Historic District
moments.text: Rowlesburg’s historic district extends beyond its commercial blocks into the surrounding residential areas. It contains 51 contributing buildings and one contributing site. Most commercial buildings have two stories, built in frame or masonry, and date from about 1900 to 1950. The district includes the Rowlesburg Area Historical Society/IOOF building of 1875 and the Adams and Moore Store building of 1907. Churches are part of it too, including Trinity Methodist Episcopal Church, dated 1915, and St. Paul’s Methodist Protestant Church, dated 1923. The district received its National Register designation in 2005.
moments.notice: Most commercial buildings are two-story frame or masonry structures.
